1.7 Basic Game Theory

What a game is

Section titled “What a game is”

The competitive firm of 1.5 Producer Theory does not need to think about its rivals: it simply takes the market price. The oligopolists of 1.6 Market Structure are different: a firm’s profit depends on how much its rivals produce and what prices they set, and the rivals’ profits depend on it too. A situation in which the payoffs of several decision makers depend on each other’s choices is called a game.

A game has three elements:

  • Players: the people or firms that make decisions.
  • Strategies: the choices each player can make.
  • Payoffs: what each player gets for every combination of choices.

Start with players who decide at the same time without seeing each other’s choices. Example: two airlines, A and B, compete on the same route, and each year each decides whether to set a high fare or a low fare. If both set high fares, each earns 10 million dollars, as with collusion in the Cournot model; if one cuts its fare, it takes most of the passengers from the other; if both cut, each earns only 5 million dollars. A table of all the combinations is called a payoff matrix. In each cell, the first number is A’s profit and the second is B’s (million dollars per year):

B: highB: low
A: high10, 102, 15
A: low15, 25, 5

What will the two airlines choose?

Dominant strategies and the prisoner’s dilemma

Section titled “Dominant strategies and the prisoner’s dilemma”

Put yourself in A’s place and consider each of B’s two choices:

  • If B sets a high fare: A gets 10 with a high fare and 15 with a low fare, so low is better.
  • If B sets a low fare: A gets 2 with a high fare and 5 with a low fare, so low is again better.

Whatever B chooses, the low fare gives A a higher profit. A strategy that is better than the player’s other strategies whatever the others choose is called a dominant strategy. B’s position is exactly symmetric, so the low fare is its dominant strategy as well. Both set low fares and earn 5 each.

The strange part is that both would earn 10 with high fares, which is better for both. Each airline makes the choice that is best for itself, yet the result is worse for everyone than another outcome. Such a game is called a prisoner’s dilemma. The name comes from a story: two suspects are questioned separately, and each can confess or stay silent; whatever the partner does, confessing gives a lighter sentence, so both confess and get heavier sentences than if both had stayed silent.

The root of the dilemma is that the outcome that is good for both requires each side to give up a choice that is better for itself, and there is no way to make sure the other side does the same. Cartel agreements are illegal in many countries and cannot be enforced in court, so the colluding firms of 1.6 Market Structure always have a reason to produce more in secret. Similar examples are advertising wars between rivals (both would be better off without advertising, but each wants to advertise a little more), and the speed race among high-frequency trading firms on exchanges (they all spend heavily to save a few microseconds, and their positions relative to each other do not change).

Check C1
A large chain A and a small shop B each decide whether to advertise. The payoffs (A, B) are: neither advertises (50, 20); A does not, B does (40, 25); A does, B does not (55, 18); both advertise (45, 15).
(a) Who has a dominant strategy, and what is it?
(b) Predict what the two firms will choose, and explain.
(c) Is this game a prisoner's dilemma?

Nash equilibrium

Section titled “Nash equilibrium”

Many games have no dominant strategy: a player’s best choice depends on what the others choose.

Example: A and B each have 100 dollars deposited in a bank. The bank has lent the deposits to a long-term project. If both wait until the project matures before withdrawing, each gets 140 dollars. If someone withdraws early, the bank must sell assets at a low price: the person who withdraws early gets back 100 dollars and the one who waits has only 60 dollars left. If both withdraw early, the assets sell for only 160 dollars in total, 80 dollars each.

B: waitB: withdraw early
A: wait140, 14060, 100
A: withdraw early100, 6080, 80

In A’s place: if B waits, A is better off waiting too (140 > 100); if B withdraws early, A is better off withdrawing early too (80 > 60). The choice that is best for a player given the others’ choices is called a best response. Here A’s best response is “do what the other does”, so A has no dominant strategy.

A combination of strategies in which each player’s strategy is a best response to the others’, so that no one wants to change alone, is called a Nash equilibrium. In this example, “both wait” is a Nash equilibrium: if the other waits, switching to an early withdrawal gives only 100, less than 140. “Both withdraw early” is also a Nash equilibrium: if the other withdraws, switching to waiting leaves only 60, less than 80.

Which of the two equilibria occurs depends on what each person expects the others to do. As long as depositors believe that others will withdraw, withdrawing is the rational choice even if the bank itself is sound, and everyone withdrawing then really does put the bank in trouble. This is a bank run: the expectation fulfills itself. In March 2023, depositors withdrew a large share of Silicon Valley Bank’s deposits within a day or two, and regulators took the bank over immediately.

The idea of Nash equilibrium applies to every game. The Cournot equilibrium of 1.6 Market Structure is a Nash equilibrium: each firm’s output is a best response to its rival’s output. If every player has a dominant strategy, how is the combination of dominant strategies related to Nash equilibrium? Prove it in Exercises Question 1. Some games (for example, a penalty kick in which the kicker picks a side and the goalkeeper guesses a side) have no such equilibrium in pure strategies, and the players must choose at random; this course does not cover that case.

Check C2
Two firms each choose technology standard X or Y for a new product. With the same standard their products are compatible: if both choose X the payoffs (A, B) are (30, 20), and if both choose Y they are (20, 30); with different standards each gets 5.
(a) Does anyone have a dominant strategy?
(b) Find all the Nash equilibria, and explain for each why no one wants to change alone.
(c) Can you predict which equilibrium will occur?

Sequential moves and backward induction

Section titled “Sequential moves and backward induction”

In some games the players move one after another, and later movers can see the earlier choices. Example: a market has a single incumbent firm, and a new firm is considering whether to enter. The incumbent announces: “If you come in, we will start a price war.” Should the new firm believe it?

A game with sequential moves can be drawn as a game tree: starting from the left, each node is a decision, each branch is a choice, and the ends show the payoffs of both sides.

The way to analyze it is to work back from the last step. Suppose the new firm has entered: the incumbent gets 30 from a price war and 50 from accommodating, so it accommodates. The new firm foresees this: entering gives 20 and staying out gives 0, so it enters. Starting from the last decision, finding the best choice at each step and then moving back is called backward induction.

The incumbent’s threat is not credible: when the time comes, carrying it out would hurt the incumbent itself. The incumbent would prefer the new firm to stay out (it would get 100), but announcing a threat does not achieve that. To make the threat credible, the incumbent must change its own payoffs in advance so that a price war really would be better for it when the time comes, for example by building very large capacity ahead of time, so that expanding output after an entry costs little. Such a prior commitment is exactly one source of barriers to entry.

Check C3
Before the entry game of Figure 4-1, the incumbent can first build a large plant. After building it (with the plant's cost already subtracted), the payoffs (entrant, incumbent) become: stay out (0, 90); enter and price war (−10, 40); enter and accommodate (20, 35).
(a) After building, if the new firm enters, what will the incumbent do? Will the new firm enter?
(b) Should the incumbent build the plant? Compare its final payoff with and without the plant.

Repeated games

Section titled “Repeated games”

Back to the airlines. If the two airlines competed only once, the prisoner’s dilemma says that both would set low fares. But they compete on the same route every year. The same game played period after period is called a repeated game.

With repetition, today’s choice affects the rival’s choices tomorrow. Suppose both airlines use this strategy: start with a high fare; keep the high fare as long as the rival has always set a high fare; once the rival sets a low fare even once, set low fares forever. This is called a trigger strategy.

Now A considers whether to cut its fare in secret this year. Compare two paths:

  • Keep the high fare: earn 10 every year.
  • Cut the fare this year: earn 15 this year, but B sets low fares forever from next year, so A earns only 5 every year after that.

Future profits must be discounted. Let the yearly discount factor be δ\deltaδ (δ=11+r\delta = \frac{1}{1+r}δ=1+r1​; if the game may end in any year, δ\deltaδ is also multiplied by the probability that it continues). The total present values today of the two paths are

10+10δ+10δ2+⋯=101−δ10 + 10\delta + 10\delta^2 + \cdots = \frac{10}{1-\delta}10+10δ+10δ2+⋯=1−δ10​

and

15+5δ+5δ2+⋯=15+5δ1−δ15 + 5\delta + 5\delta^2 + \cdots = 15 + \frac{5\delta}{1-\delta}15+5δ+5δ2+⋯=15+1−δ5δ​

(This is the sum of a geometric series, derived in the same way as the perpetuity, except that the first payment is today.) The gain from cutting the fare comes now and the cost comes later, so the conclusion depends on δ\deltaδ, that is, on how much the airline values the future.

How large must δ\deltaδ be for keeping the high fare to pay? Use the figure to answer Check C4; the general condition is derived in Exercises Question 2. The comparison shows that cooperation is easier to sustain when the players value the future, the game is likely to continue, cheating is detected and punished quickly, and the gain from cheating once is small. What happens if everyone knows the game ends in a certain period? See Exercises Question 4.

Repeated games also explain why reputation has value. Banks, market makers and investment advisers deal with their clients again and again, and the short-term gain from cheating once is outweighed by the business lost later. Conversely, a counterparty in a one-time deal needs to be held in check by contracts, regulation or collateral.

In Figure 5-1, raise δ\deltaδ step by step and find the smallest δ\deltaδ at which keeping the high price is at least as good as cutting the price now. Then compute the exact value from the lesson's two present-value expressions. Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • A game consists of players, strategies and payoffs; a game with simultaneous moves is shown as a payoff matrix.
  • Dominant strategy: a strategy that is better whatever the rival chooses. Prisoner’s dilemma: each side’s dominant strategy leads to an outcome worse for everyone.
  • Nash equilibrium: each player’s strategy is a best response to the others’, so no one wants to change alone. A game can have several Nash equilibria; in a bank run, for example, which one occurs depends on expectations.
  • Games with sequential moves are solved by backward induction; a threat that would hurt the threatener when the time comes is not credible, and a prior commitment can make it credible.
  • In a repeated game, trigger strategies can sustain cooperation; whether cooperation pays depends on the discount factor δ\deltaδ.

Exercises

Section titled “Exercises”
Question 1
True or false? Explain. If every player has a strictly dominant strategy (strictly better than the player's other strategies whatever the others choose), then the profile in which everyone plays the dominant strategy is a Nash equilibrium, and it is the only Nash equilibrium.
Question 2 ★
A general prisoner's dilemma: if both cooperate, each gets RRR; if you defect while the other cooperates, you get TTT; if both defect, each gets PPP; if you cooperate while the other defects, you get SSS, with T>R>P>ST > R > P > ST>R>P>S. The game is repeated forever, both use trigger strategies, and the discount factor is δ\deltaδ.
(a) Show that continuing to cooperate is at least as good as defecting now if and only if δ≥T−RT−P\delta \ge \frac{T - R}{T - P}δ≥T−PT−R​.
(b) Use this condition to explain how the temptation to defect (T−RT - RT−R) and the severity of the punishment (R−PR - PR−P) affect whether cooperation can be sustained.
(c) Substitute the airline numbers from the lesson and check against the result of Check C4.
Question 3
In the lesson's bank-run example, the government introduces deposit insurance: if a depositor who waits until maturity gets less than ggg dollars, the insurer tops it up to ggg.
(a) How large must ggg be at least for "both withdraw early" to stop being a Nash equilibrium? Is "wait" then a dominant strategy?
(b) In the new equilibrium, does the insurer have to pay anything? What does this show about how deposit insurance works?
Question 4
The two airlines in the lesson both know that the route will close in exactly 10 years, after which they will have no further dealings.
(a) Use backward induction to show that both price low in every year.
(b) In reality many industries do not last forever either, yet tacit cooperation between firms often lasts a long time. Give an explanation using the concepts of this lesson.
